docs.title: Clichy engineering guide
docs.text:
Clichy is a self-hosted photo library service developed for ECAM Brussels Project 2026. This site documents the implementation visible in this repository, the current Kubernetes and CI configuration, and the gaps against the assignment. It is intended for developers, operators, and evaluation preparation.

Repository state, not a live cluster audit

Statements about implementation are based on the checked-out source and Git history. Unless explicitly stated, this documentation has not verified the current state of a live cluster. See the requirements matrix for status definitions.

Start with the project overview, then follow developer onboarding. Operators should read the Kubernetes environments, deployment runbook, and database migration guide.

The source review is based on the checked-out repository; the application contains a web UI, authenticated API, filesystem photo storage, image metadata and hashing, and asynchronous processing. CNPG is configured in repository manifests for two PostgreSQL instances per environment, but installation, replication and failover on valtask have not been verified. Redis remains one instance per namespace; sharding is not configured. Production traffic is proxied by Cloudflare for valtask.xyz and www.valtask.xyz and delivered to the server through Cloudflare Tunnel before Traefik.

docs.title: Web
docs.text: apps/web is a React Router application built with Vite. File-system route setup is in apps/web/src/routes.ts; visible routes include index, login, and dashboard. Components include login/sign-up forms and user menu. The browser API origin is supplied through VITE_SERVER_URL; production image build currently passes http://localhost:3000, so deployments that need another public API origin must review the build argument and routing assumptions.

docs.title: API and authentication
docs.text:
apps/server/src/index.ts creates a Fastify server on port 3000, enables multipart uploads (20 MiB maximum), CORS with credentials, exposes /metrics, mounts photo routes, and adapts Better Auth under /api/auth/*. Better Auth uses Prisma/PostgreSQL and email/password auth. Fastify's logger is enabled. Route handlers return explicit errors for unauthenticated requests, missing input, unsupported images, and missing records; unexpected errors are passed to Fastify's handler.

Key routes in apps/server/src/routes/photos.ts:

Method/path Purpose GET /photos List the authenticated user's photos POST /photos Validate and save upload; create record and return 202 pending processing GET /photos/:id/metadata Read metadata for an owned photo GET /photos/:id/thumbnail/:variant Read an owned derivative variant GET /photos/:id Retrieve original photo content GET /photos/:id/duplicates Find exact SHA-256 matches owned by the user GET /photos/:id/similar Rank candidates by pHash distance; accepts threshold and limit DELETE /photos/:id Delete an owned photo and its stored files

Auth route surface is Better Auth's handler; consult packages/auth/src/index.ts and Better Auth config for exact behavior.

docs.title: Image pipeline
docs.text:
apps/server/src/image-processing.ts validates and decodes JPEG, PNG, WebP, and GIF using Sharp with a 40-million-pixel cap. It extracts optional EXIF via Exifr, generates SHA-256 and a 64-bit DCT perceptual hash, and writes resized WebP variants. pHash comparison uses Hamming distance in query helpers; this is a similarity primitive, not evidence of a complete duplicate review interface. Video support was not found.

apps/server/src/storage.ts implements local filesystem storage. Production mounts the same photos PVC into API and worker. This storage design makes shared writable filesystem semantics a runtime dependency.

docs.title: Error handling and logging
docs.text: Fastify logger handles API logs; worker logs structured JSON to stdout/stderr. Image validation errors and missing original files are permanent BullMQ failures; other errors can retry. Tests are Node test runner via tsx --test; test files are colocated in server and worker packages. No dedicated lint script is declared at root.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant API as Fastify API
  participant DB as PostgreSQL
  participant D as Outbox dispatcher (in API)
  participant R as Redis / BullMQ
  participant W as Worker
  participant FS as Photo filesystem
  U->>API: POST /photos (multipart)
  API->>API: Validate image and persist original
  API->>DB: Transaction: photo row + outbox row
  API-->>U: 202 Accepted, PENDING
  D->>DB: Read unpublished outbox batch
  D->>R: Add process-photo with stable job ID
  D->>DB: Mark event published (or retain error)
  R->>W: Deliver job
  W->>DB: Atomically claim PENDING/FAILED photo
  W->>FS: Read original; write derivatives
  W->>DB: Store EXIF, dimensions, hashes, COMPLETED

The outbox reduces the chance that a database photo row is committed while its queue event is lost. Dispatcher logic is in apps/server/src/queues/outbox-dispatcher.ts; upload transaction is wired in apps/server/src/routes/photos.ts. A stable SHA-256-derived job ID makes repeated publication idempotent at the queue identity level.

The original file is written before the database transaction. If the API process stops after the filesystem write but before the transaction commits, there is no photo row or outbox event to recover, and the repository has no orphan-file sweeper. When database registration returns an error, the route attempts to delete the original and logs cleanup failures, but that cleanup is best-effort.

BullMQ defaults: four attempts, exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds, completed job retention up to one day/1000 jobs, failed up to seven days/5000 jobs. These can be set using PHOTO_JOB_ATTEMPTS, PHOTO_JOB_BACKOFF_MS; queue name defaults to photo-processing. Worker concurrency supports 1 or 2 in code; current overlays set 1.

Worker marks invalid images or missing originals as terminal failures, and transient errors return the photo to pending for retry. The server dispatcher retries failed outbox publication; it runs every two seconds, recovers processing records older than 15 minutes and pending records older than 10 minutes, and removes published outbox rows after seven days. If the worker is killed abruptly, the photo stays PROCESSING until stale-processing recovery runs; allow at least 15 minutes before expecting the outbox to republish it. A normal SIGTERM instead lets BullMQ close gracefully and finish its active job within Kubernetes' 120-second termination grace period.

The worker exposes HTTP health on port 3001. The Deployment configures a liveness probe on /live and a readiness probe on /ready; readiness also requires the Redis connection to be ready. After BullMQ exhausts its retries, or finds an invalid image or missing original, the photo remains FAILED; there is no per-photo retry action in the UI. The operator can run the backfill script to reschedule incomplete photos, but it scans the whole library.

Tests cover derivative creation, permanent and transient failures, a duplicate delivery losing the database claim, outbox publication failure, the enqueue/ack crash window, and stale-processing recovery. Live worker interruption and recovery still need to be demonstrated in Test.

docs.title: Networking and request flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Client[Browser / external client] -->|HTTPS: valtask.xyz or www.valtask.xyz| Proxy[Cloudflare reverse proxy]
  Proxy -->|canonical valtask.xyz route| Tunnel[cloudflared tunnel]
  Tunnel -->|HTTP inside tunnel to Traefik port 80| Ingress[Traefik Ingress: entrypoint web]
  Proxy -. 301 www to canonical valtask.xyz .-> Client
  Ingress -->|/| WebSvc[ClusterIP clichy-web:80]
  Ingress -->|/api/auth, /photos| ApiSvc[ClusterIP clichy-server:3000]
  WebSvc --> WebPod[web Pod]
  ApiSvc --> ApiPod[server Pod]
  ApiPod -->|clichy-postgres-rw:5432| PG[CNPG primary Service]
  ApiPod -->|clichy-redis:6379| Redis[Redis Service]
  WorkerPod[worker Pod] --> PG
  WorkerPod --> Redis
  WorkerPod --> SharedPV[(photo PVC)]
  ApiPod --> SharedPV

The base Ingress uses Traefik class and the web entrypoint. It sends /api/auth and /photos to the API and / to web. Environment overlays change the hostname: clichy.localhost (Dev), clichy-test.home.arpa (Test), valtask.xyz (Production). In Production, Cloudflare acts as the public reverse proxy for both valtask.xyz and www.valtask.xyz; the configured Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) carries requests to Traefik on port 80 before they reach the Kubernetes Services and Pods. Cloudflare terminates public HTTPS. The www hostname is redirected to the canonical https://valtask.xyz host at the proxy/tunnel edge; the Kubernetes Ingress handles the canonical host. Tunnel, DNS and redirect configuration are external to this repository. The repo's current base ingress annotation selects web; TLS configuration is not present in that Ingress.

Services use namespace-local DNS names (clichy-postgres-rw, clichy-redis, clichy-server, clichy-web). PostgreSQL and Redis are ClusterIP internal services; no public database/Redis ingress or service is configured. For local access, use the documented ingress route or explicit kubectl port-forward only when needed.

docs.title: Network diagram caveat
docs.text: The separate Ingress resources for Grafana and Headlamp are under infra/kubernetes/monitoring and infra/kubernetes/headlamp; they are LAN-oriented configuration. They are not included in the application Ingress and are not exposed by the documented Cloudflare Tunnel. Check their host/entrypoint and cluster DNS before assuming reachability.

docs.title: Current deployment view
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  User[Browser] -->|HTTPS valtask.xyz or www.valtask.xyz| Proxy[Cloudflare reverse proxy]
  Proxy -->|routes canonical valtask.xyz requests| Tunnel[cloudflared tunnel]
  Proxy -. www redirects to canonical valtask.xyz .-> User
  Tunnel -->|HTTP to Traefik web :80| Traefik[Traefik Ingress]
  subgraph AppNS[Clichy-prod namespace]
    Traefik -->|/| Web[web Deployment]
    Traefik -->|/api/auth and /photos| API[server Deployment]
    API -->|Prisma via clichy-postgres-rw| PG[CNPG primary]
    PG -->|asynchronous WAL streaming| PGReplica[CNPG standby]
    PG --> PGV1[(Primary PVC)]
    PGReplica --> PGV2[(Standby PVC)]
    API -->|BullMQ| Redis[(Redis Deployment, 1 replica + AOF PVC)]
    API -->|original + derivative files| Photos[(photos PVC)]
    API -. DB outbox dispatcher .-> Redis
    Worker[worker Deployment] --> Redis
    Worker --> PG
    Worker --> Photos
  end
  Prom[Prometheus in monitoring namespace] -. /metrics .-> API
  Prom -. CNPG exporter .-> PG
  Grafana[Grafana] --> Prom

The public Production request path begins at Cloudflare, which is the reverse proxy for both valtask.xyz and www.valtask.xyz. HTTPS terminates there; cloudflared forwards the requests through the tunnel as HTTP to Traefik's web entrypoint on port 80. Cloudflare redirects www.valtask.xyz to canonical valtask.xyz; the application Ingress host is valtask.xyz. Tunnel, DNS and redirect rules are configured outside this repository. Traefik then routes the UI and API paths to their in-cluster Services.

The server is both the HTTP API and outbox dispatcher. It constructs the BullMQ queue and periodically dispatches pending outbox entries. Worker instances consume process-photo jobs. The API and worker need the same photo files; Kubernetes mounts the photos PVC into both Deployments.

docs.title: Namespace interpretation
docs.text: The repository defines clichy-dev, clichy-test, and clichy-prod; monitoring and Headlamp are separate cluster-level installations/namespaces. These are namespace boundaries on one cluster, not separate clusters. Each environment overlay defines an independent two-instance CNPG database cluster and independent application Secrets; Redis remains a separate Deployment.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The repository configures one server, web, and worker replica by default (Test has an HPA for server/web), one Redis instance, and two PostgreSQL instances per namespace. CNPG replication, failover, and metrics are configured but remain unverified until applied on the live cluster. PostgreSQL is not sharded. Both database instances and their independent node-local volumes remain on the same physical host; this does not provide node-level availability. The old Production PostgreSQL PV is retained during migration.

docs.title: Repository status
docs.text: No automated PostgreSQL dump, WAL archive, snapshot schedule, restore script, or documented tested restore procedure is present in the checked-in implementation. Persistent volumes and Retain reclaim policy do not constitute a backup. Photo originals also live outside PostgreSQL and must be backed up consistently with their database references.

docs.title: Operational requirement
docs.text:
Until a validated procedure exists, treat backup/restore as an open operational gap. Design a coordinated backup covering PostgreSQL and photo storage, define retention and encryption, and test restores into an isolated namespace. Preserve Redis only as appropriate for queue recovery; the database outbox and stale-record recovery are relevant to re-enqueueing work, but are not backups.

Do not run ad hoc destructive recovery commands against Production. A future runbook should record approved tooling, consistency point, secret handling, validation queries, and recovery time/data objectives without storing credentials in the repository.

docs.title: Local workflow
docs.text:
Edit the Prisma schema, then use:

pnpm db:generate
pnpm db:migrate

The root db:migrate delegates to @clichy/db and runs prisma migrate dev; it can create a migration and prompt in development. Review and commit the generated SQL under packages/db/prisma/migrations with the schema change. pnpm db:push is available but bypasses migration history; do not use it for production changes.

Inspect migration state:

pnpm --filter @clichy/db exec prisma migrate status
./infra/kubernetes/scripts/migrate.sh test status
./infra/kubernetes/scripts/migrate.sh prod status

The environment script uses the namespace Secret and loopback port-forward. It does not print the DB URL. Running status can return nonzero when migrations are pending.

docs.title: Deployment ordering
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  SHA[Checked out SHA + matching immutable images] --> Verify[Verify clean source, node and target Secret]
  Verify --> Ready[Wait for CNPG Cluster Ready]
  Ready --> Forward[Loopback port-forward through clichy-postgres-rw and PostgreSQL SELECT 1]
  Forward --> Migrate[prisma migrate deploy]
  Migrate -->|success| Apply[Render and apply environment Kustomize overlay]
  Migrate -->|failure| Stop[Stop; app manifests not applied]
  Apply --> Rollout[Wait for server, web, worker rollouts]

The workflow applies migrations before deploying the matching app images. The migration script confirms the target database name (clichy_test or clichy_prod) from the connection URL and checks commit cleanliness for relevant sources. Because old Pods may serve while DDL runs, use backward-compatible expand-and-contract migrations. No transactional rollback or automatic schema rollback is provided; Prisma migration failures require diagnosis and a forward repair plan.

docs.title: PostgreSQL and Prisma
docs.text:
CNPG 1.30.1 with PostgreSQL 18.6 provides two-instance clusters in Dev, Test, and Production for physical replication exercises. Dev and Production applications use CNPG's clichy-postgres-rw Service. Test additionally runs a separate single-node Citus 14.2/PostgreSQL 18 database, and the Test application uses clichy-citus-rw for its logically sharded photo tables. The Test CNPG cluster remains available for replication demonstrations. See Citus sharding for scope and limitations.

Production's operator and two-instance Cluster are deployed on valtask. The evidence currently recorded confirms Cluster readiness and database connectivity, but does not yet include a live WAL sender/receiver query or a failover exercise. Check those using the Replication runbook. Dev/Test live status should be verified separately. Both instances use separate PVCs but remain on the same physical node. This provides practice with PostgreSQL replication and Pod/storage recovery, not protection against loss of valtask.

CNPG 1.30.1 supports Kubernetes 1.34–1.36; Kubernetes 1.37 has been tested by the release but is not listed as officially supported. The repository's K3s installer targets 1.37, and K3s itself is not a Kubernetes distribution covered by CNPG's vanilla-Kubernetes support policy. The pinned installer requires an explicit opt-in for a 1.37 server. See the official support matrix.

Prisma 7 schema is split across packages/db/prisma/schema/auth.prisma and photo.prisma. prisma.config.ts points at the migration directory and reads DATABASE_URL; client generation outputs under packages/db/prisma/generated. createPrismaClient in packages/db/src/index.ts uses the PostgreSQL adapter against CNPG or Citus.

The schema contains Better Auth user/session/account/verification tables, Photo metadata and processing state, and PhotoProcessingOutbox. Photo and outbox keys include userId so Citus can colocate each user's rows. Photo indexes include user ownership, per-user SHA and perceptual hashes, processing state/start time, and deletion marker. Originals and derivatives are files on a PVC; the database stores storage keys and metadata, not photo bytes.

Migrations are committed under packages/db/prisma/migrations. See migration workflow, replication status, sharding status, and backup gaps.

docs.title: Current state
docs.text:
CloudNativePG (CNPG) is configured for two PostgreSQL 18.6 instances in each app namespace. In Production on valtask, the cluster has been observed Ready with two running instances, and the application database connection has been restored. The primary/standby roles and WAL streaming are configured, but the evidence collected so far does not include a live pg_stat_replication result or a failover test. Dev and Test live status should be checked separately.

The old PostgreSQL StatefulSet is no longer included in the environment overlays. Its existing production PV and data directory are retained and are not reused by CNPG. CNPG provisions one independent PVC per instance. Production uses two pre-bound, retained local PVs; Dev and Test use K3s local-path dynamic provisioning. The operator affinity retains preferred anti-affinity, allowing both instances on this one-node cluster while still preferring separation if nodes are added later.

docs.title: Architecture and WAL flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  App[API, worker, Prisma migrations] -->|TCP 5432| RW[CNPG -rw Service]
  RW --> Primary[Primary Pod: reads and writes]
  Primary -->|WAL stream, asynchronous| Standby[Standby Pod: recovery/read-only]
  Primary --> PVC1[(PVC: primary data)]
  Standby --> PVC2[(PVC: standby data)]
  Operator[CNPG operator] -. watches, repairs, promotes .-> Primary
  Operator -. watches, repairs, promotes .-> Standby

CNPG configures and supervises the PostgreSQL instances; PostgreSQL itself streams write-ahead log (WAL) records from the primary and replays them on the standby. Asynchronous replication is selected (minSyncReplicas: 0, maxSyncReplicas: 0): writes do not wait for standby acknowledgement, so a sudden primary loss can lose the most recent unreceived transactions. Synchronous replication waits for configured standbys and can reduce that loss window, but adds write latency and can block writes when acknowledgers are unavailable; it is not enabled here.

CNPG runs a controller in cnpg-system, exposes clichy-postgres-rw and read-only -ro/-r role services, and reconciles the cluster resource. The app uses only -rw; no replica read routing is configured. CNPG promotes an eligible standby after it determines the primary has failed, updates the role service, and recreates/rejoins the former primary as a standby when possible. A deliberate Pod deletion tests the controller's Pod failure recovery path, but it is not equivalent to loss of the node or a controlled PostgreSQL shutdown.

This single-node prototype does not protect against power, disk, OS, K3s, or physical server failure. Replication is not a backup: accidental deletes and logical corruption can be replayed. Keep backups and tested restore as separate work.

docs.title: Install and inspect
docs.text:
The pinned operator installer is infra/kubernetes/cnpg/install-operator.sh. CNPG 1.30.1 officially supports Kubernetes 1.34–1.36; its release is tested but not officially supported on 1.37. The project K3s installer currently targets 1.37, so check the live server version first. The script refuses 1.37 unless the operator explicitly opts in with CNPG_ALLOW_TESTED_UNSUPPORTED_K8S=1; K3s distribution support is also outside CNPG's formal vanilla-Kubernetes support policy. Do not interpret successful install as upstream support.

On valtask, from a clean checkout of this repository, check kubectl version -o json and /srv/clichy free space first. The supplied host report had 28 GiB free on that 30 GiB filesystem; the new two 2 GiB CNPG volumes are separate from the retained legacy volume. Then install the operator once:

# For Kubernetes 1.34–1.36:
./infra/kubernetes/cnpg/install-operator.sh

# Only if the actual server reports Kubernetes 1.37 and you accept the
# tested-but-not-supported status:
CNPG_ALLOW_TESTED_UNSUPPORTED_K8S=1 ./infra/kubernetes/cnpg/install-operator.sh

The installation creates the cnpg-system namespace, CRDs, RBAC and operator Deployment. Next, create fresh empty DB clusters and credentials; this prepares secrets, local PV directories for Prod, and CNPG resources, but does not remove or import legacy database contents:

./infra/kubernetes/scripts/prepare-namespace.sh test
./infra/kubernetes/scripts/prepare-namespace.sh dev
./infra/kubernetes/scripts/prepare-namespace.sh prod

Each script prompts before changing its namespace and may prompt for GHCR credentials if needed. The Prod run creates /srv/clichy/k3s-storage/prod/postgres-cnpg-1 and -2 only when absent/empty, sets UID/GID 26 on new paths, and retains /srv/clichy/k3s-storage/prod/postgres. Once Test is Ready, push the reviewed commit through the ordinary pipeline: CI runs tests/builds, deploys Test, and the configured Production environment gate controls Prod promotion. deploy.sh refuses to migrate or deploy until CNPG reports Ready.

After operator install and namespace preparation, inspect roles and PVCs:

kubectl get cluster,pods,svc,pvc -n clichy-prod -o wide
kubectl get pods -n clichy-prod -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres -L cnpg.io/instanceRole
kubectl get endpointslice -n clichy-prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=clichy-postgres-rw
kubectl describe cluster clichy-postgres -n clichy-prod

kubectl cnpg status clichy-postgres -n clichy-prod is also useful if the optional CNPG kubectl plugin is installed; it is not installed by the operator script.

Connect with psql using the in-cluster clichy-postgres-rw Service and the clichy-postgres-app credentials (do not put passwords directly in shell history). On the primary, inspect active senders:

SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn
FROM pg_stat_replication;

On the standby, check recovery and WAL receive/replay positions:

SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();

The primary should return false for pg_is_in_recovery() and list a streaming standby in pg_stat_replication. The standby should return true; receive/replay positions should advance after writes. pg_stat_replication is queried on the primary; it does not show the standby from itself.

For a quick live check on Production, query the primary from its Pod:

NS=clichy-prod
PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" \
  -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres,cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec -n "$NS" "$PRIMARY" -- psql -U postgres -d postgres -c \
  "SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, sent_lsn, replay_lsn, \
   pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn)::bigint) AS byte_lag \
   FROM pg_stat_replication;"

Expect one row for the standby with state = streaming and sync_state = async. A NULL lag can occur when there is no recent WAL activity; the streaming state is the key check. This command reads status only and does not change the cluster.

docs.title: Demonstrate replication and failover (Test only)
docs.text:
Run these steps on valtask with the context explicitly set to the intended cluster. Every state-changing command below targets clichy-test; do not copy it with a Production namespace. Confirm the cluster is healthy and has exactly one primary and one replica before starting:

NS=clichy-test
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get cluster clichy-postgres -n "$NS" -o wide
kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres -L cnpg.io/instanceRole -o wide
kubectl get pvc -n "$NS" -o wide
PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres,cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
REPLICA=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres,cnpg.io/instanceRole=replica -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
test -n "$PRIMARY" && test -n "$REPLICA" && test "$PRIMARY" != "$REPLICA"
printf 'primary=%s replica=%s namespace=%s\n' "$PRIMARY" "$REPLICA" "$NS"

On the primary, verify its role and WAL sender. On the replica, verify recovery mode and receiver/replay positions:

kubectl exec -n "$NS" "$PRIMARY" -- psql -U postgres -d postgres -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c \
  "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();" \
  -c "SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, sent_lsn, replay_lsn FROM pg_stat_replication;"
kubectl exec -n "$NS" "$REPLICA" -- psql -U postgres -d postgres -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c \
  "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();"

The primary must report false and one sender in streaming state; the replica must report true. To prove replay, create a disposable marker on the primary and poll the read-only replica until asynchronous WAL replay catches up:

kubectl exec -n "$NS" "$PRIMARY" -- psql -U postgres -d clichy_test -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c \
  "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cnpg_replication_demo; CREATE TABLE cnpg_replication_demo (id integer PRIMARY KEY, marker text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO cnpg_replication_demo VALUES (1, 'wal-check');"
for attempt in $(seq 1 30); do
  if kubectl exec -n "$NS" "$REPLICA" -- psql -U postgres -d clichy_test -Atqc \
    "SELECT marker FROM cnpg_replication_demo WHERE id = 1;" | grep -qx wal-check; then
    echo "WAL marker replayed on $REPLICA"
    break
  fi
  if [ "$attempt" -eq 30 ]; then
    echo "WAL marker did not appear on the replica within 30 seconds" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  sleep 1
done

Wait until the replica returns the marker before switching; this avoids testing with an un-replayed asynchronous write. If the optional CNPG kubectl plugin is installed, request a planned switchover. The plugin is not installed by the repository's operator installer. If the command reports unknown command "cnpg", skip this planned-switchover substep and continue with the automatic failover exercise below:

kubectl cnpg promote clichy-postgres "$REPLICA" -n "$NS"
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready cluster.postgresql.cnpg.io/clichy-postgres \
  -n "$NS" --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres -L cnpg.io/instanceRole -o wide
kubectl get endpointslice -n "$NS" -l kubernetes.io/service-name=clichy-postgres-rw -o wide

After a successful promote command, confirm that the former replica is now primary and that the -rw EndpointSlice points to it. For an actual Prisma CLI write through clichy-postgres-rw, open a loopback-only port-forward in Terminal A and leave it running while you execute the commands in Terminal B:

kubectl port-forward --address=127.0.0.1 -n clichy-test service/clichy-postgres-rw 15432:5432

In Terminal B, load the Test-only local secrets file created by prepare-namespace.sh (the commands do not print its contents), point Prisma at the local forwarded port, and create a uniquely named disposable table using Prisma:

set -a
source "$HOME/.config/clichy/test-secrets.env"
set +a
test "$(node -e 'console.log(new URL(process.env.DATABASE_URL).pathname.slice(1))')" = clichy_test
DATABASE_URL="$(node -e '
  const url = new URL(process.env.DATABASE_URL);
  if (url.hostname !== "clichy-postgres-rw" || url.pathname !== "/clichy_test") process.exit(1);
  url.hostname = "127.0.0.1";
  url.port = "15432";
  url.searchParams.set("sslmode", "disable");
  process.stdout.write(url.toString());
')"
export DATABASE_URL
PSQL_URL="$(node -e '
  const url = new URL(process.env.DATABASE_URL);
  url.searchParams.delete("schema");
  url.searchParams.set("sslmode", "disable");
  process.stdout.write(url.toString());
')"
export PSQL_URL
pnpm --filter @clichy/db exec prisma db execute --stdin <<'SQL'
CREATE TABLE cnpg_prisma_failover_demo (id integer PRIMARY KEY, marker text NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO cnpg_prisma_failover_demo VALUES (1, 'after-switchover');
SQL
psql "$PSQL_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c \
  "SELECT * FROM cnpg_prisma_failover_demo ORDER BY id;"
psql "$PSQL_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c \
  "DROP TABLE cnpg_prisma_failover_demo;"
unset DATABASE_URL PSQL_URL POSTGRES_PASSWORD

prisma db execute reads its datasource from prisma.config.ts; it does not accept --schema. PSQL_URL removes Prisma's schema query parameter because libpq rejects it. Both connections go through the clichy-postgres-rw port-forward. Prisma creates and inserts the row, then psql reads it back before cleanup. ./infra/kubernetes/scripts/migrate.sh test status is an additional Prisma connectivity/migration check; it is read-only and does not prove a write. Stop Terminal A with Ctrl-C after Terminal B completes.

If the evaluation specifically requires automatic failover after primary loss, perform this exercise after the replication marker was observed and the cluster is healthy. If you also ran a planned switchover, first confirm that it completed and the cluster returned Ready. This deliberately deletes the current primary Pod in Test (never its PVC), so expect a short connection interruption:

PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n clichy-test \
  -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres,cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
test -n "$PRIMARY"
printf 'About to delete Test primary Pod %s in namespace clichy-test\n' "$PRIMARY"
kubectl delete pod "$PRIMARY" -n clichy-test
kubectl get pods -n clichy-test -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres \
  -L cnpg.io/instanceRole -w

Stop the watch once both Pods are Ready and the role label has moved to the former replica. Then check the Cluster and -rw endpoint separately:

kubectl get cluster clichy-postgres -n clichy-test -o wide
kubectl get endpointslice -n clichy-test \
  -l kubernetes.io/service-name=clichy-postgres-rw -o wide

Re-run the recovery and sender checks above. Recompute PRIMARY and REPLICA from labels because CNPG may assign different instance names, then reopen the loopback port-forward and repeat the Prisma CLI write/read check above through clichy-postgres-rw. Remove the WAL marker from the current primary when finished:

PRIMARY=$(kubectl get pod -n clichy-test -l cnpg.io/cluster=clichy-postgres,cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec -n clichy-test "$PRIMARY" -- psql -U postgres -d clichy_test -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c \
  "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cnpg_replication_demo;"

Pod deletion tests CNPG's automated response to primary Pod loss, but it does not simulate node-level HA and asynchronous replication can lose un-replayed transactions. Never delete either instance PVC. Do not perform either switchover or Pod deletion in Production for this demonstration.

docs.title: Retire the legacy StatefulSet after cutover
docs.text:
The Kustomize overlay no longer declares the legacy StatefulSet, but Kubernetes does not automatically delete resources removed from a manifest. Once the new application is verified in every environment, an operator can remove only the old StatefulSet and old Service:

kubectl delete statefulset clichy-postgres -n clichy-test
kubectl delete service clichy-postgres -n clichy-test

Repeat for Dev and Production only after checking the selected object and its namespace. Do not delete data-clichy-postgres-0, its PVC, the legacy PV, or the old directory as part of this step; retain them until intentionally cleaning up storage in a separately reviewed operation. CNPG's similarly named Cluster is clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io/clichy-postgres, not the old StatefulSet.

docs.title: Monitoring and Headlamp
docs.text: CNPG exports PostgreSQL metrics on Pod port metrics (9187). infra/kubernetes/monitoring/cnpg-pod-monitor.yaml selects CNPG Pods in all three namespaces; the Prometheus Helm values select the PodMonitor. Grafana adds role/recovery, lag, streaming replica and WAL receiver panels, and Prometheus alerts for a disconnected replica and sustained lag. Headlamp receives read-only access to clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io so its mapping can display CNPG Cluster status alongside Pods, Services and PVCs. Verify actual scrape targets in Prometheus and the panels/alerts after installation; YAML alone does not prove telemetry is flowing.

docs.title: Storage and limits
docs.text:
Each instance has an independent 2 GiB PVC in this prototype. The production manifest binds to /srv/clichy/k3s-storage/prod/postgres-cnpg-1 and -2; each path must be an empty directory owned by UID/GID 26 before first start. The supplied preparation script creates these paths without changing the legacy PostgreSQL directory. Two copies of the database consume about twice the data volume, plus WAL and filesystem overhead. The production paths share the existing 30 GiB /srv/clichy filesystem, so watch both PVC metrics and host free space. Dev/Test use dynamically provisioned local-path PVCs.

The operator can automatically recover a Pod or promote a standby, but the whole cluster remains on one K3s node. This design demonstrates the mechanics and does not provide host-level availability, geographic recovery, or a backup. Production and Test are separate PostgreSQL clusters with independent PVCs and Secrets; no Production-to-Test refresh/anonymization job is implemented.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Test uses a separate Citus 14.2 / PostgreSQL 18 database. The existing two-instance CNPG cluster remains deployed for the replication exercises; the Test application connects to clichy-citus-rw. Dev and Production continue to use CNPG directly.

This is a deliberately small single-node Citus setup. Citus divides photo metadata and processing-outbox rows into 32 logical shards by userId; rows for the same user are colocated. The Citus coordinator and all shards currently live in one PostgreSQL Pod on valtask. This demonstrates database-level logical sharding and Citus query routing, but it does not yet distribute data or failure domains across multiple database hosts.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Photo uses the compound primary key (userId, id). PhotoProcessingOutbox carries userId and uses (userId, id) as its key, with a compound foreign key to its photo. Its Citus shard key is also userId, so a user's photo and outbox event are colocated. The small user identity table is a Citus reference table, replicated by Citus for foreign-key checks. The application includes userId in worker jobs and uses compound Prisma lookups so point reads/writes identify the shard.

The Prisma migration changes keys but does not call Citus-only functions. Test, Dev, and local PostgreSQL use the compound primary keys. Production temporarily retains its existing single-column primary keys plus composite unique indexes, so the old application can keep writing during the migration-before-rollout window. Its outbox userId column remains nullable for that same transition; the new dispatcher repairs events created by the old version. Test-only distribution registration runs after Prisma migrations through infra/kubernetes/citus/enable-user-sharding.sql.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
prepare-namespace.sh test creates the Test Citus Secret credentials and applies the Citus Deployment/PVC. deploy.sh test <sha> waits for both CNPG and Citus, applies Prisma migrations through clichy-citus-rw, registers the tables with Citus, then deploys the app. The Test application Secret uses the clichy-citus-rw host. Production migrations continue through CNPG clichy-postgres-rw.

The existing Test CNPG database is retained and is not automatically copied or deleted by the Citus setup. A fresh Citus database has no existing users/photos until data is deliberately migrated or recreated. Do not remove the old CNPG cluster or its PVCs as part of this change.

docs.title: Verify on valtask
docs.text:
kubectl get deployment,pods,pvc,service -n clichy-test -l app=clichy-citus -o wide
kubectl exec -n clichy-test deployment/clichy-citus -- \
  psql -U clichy -d clichy_test -c 'SELECT citus_version();'
kubectl exec -n clichy-test deployment/clichy-citus -- \
  psql -U clichy -d clichy_test -c \
  "SELECT logicalrelid::regclass AS table_name, partmethod, partkey \
   FROM pg_dist_partition ORDER BY 1;"
kubectl exec -n clichy-test deployment/clichy-citus -- \
  psql -U clichy -d clichy_test -c \
  "SELECT p.logicalrelid::regclass AS table_name, p.partkey, \
          count(s.shardid) AS shard_count \
   FROM pg_dist_partition p \
   JOIN pg_dist_shard s USING (logicalrelid) \
   GROUP BY p.logicalrelid, p.partkey \
   ORDER BY p.logicalrelid::regclass::text;"
kubectl exec -n clichy-test deployment/clichy-citus -- \
  psql -U clichy -d clichy_test -c \
  "EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM \"Photo\" \
   WHERE \"userId\" = 'demo-user' AND id = 'demo-photo';"

To observe routing, issue a Test application photo lookup scoped by both userId and id, then inspect EXPLAIN for that query through the coordinator. A multi-worker Citus topology is a separate follow-up: it needs PostgreSQL/Citus workers, node registration and worker failure handling. Do not add that complexity until the single-node route is validated.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A single Citus Pod is a single point of failure and does not inherit CNPG failover. Its PVC provides persistence, not high availability.
  • All Citus shards currently share the same CPU, memory, storage and host. This is a functional sharding baseline, not a capacity/scaling benchmark.
  • Global queries such as dispatcher batches can touch multiple shards. User-scoped photo queries and worker jobs carry the shard key.
  • Photo bytes remain on the existing shared photos PVC; this change shards database rows, not image files.
  • Citus requires the shard key in unique constraints and colocated foreign keys. Keep Prisma migrations and Citus registration SQL aligned when changing these models.

docs.title: Architecture decision records
docs.text:
These lightweight records summarize choices visible in code and configuration. Where no formal decision record was found, the rationale is stated as repository context or an inferred explanation, not as a confirmed historical decision.

  • ADR 0001: Kubernetes and environment namespaces
  • ADR 0002: PostgreSQL and Prisma
  • ADR 0003: Redis and BullMQ
  • ADR 0004: Citus experiment
  • ADR 0007: PostgreSQL replication and sharding scope

docs.title: ADR 0001: Kubernetes and environment namespaces
docs.text: Status: Adopted in repository configuration; live operational status not independently verified.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The project targets self-hosted deployment on K3s and needs isolated Dev, Test, and Production configuration plus containerized services.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use Kubernetes resources rendered with Kustomize, K3s for the on-premise cluster setup, Traefik Ingress, and clichy-dev, clichy-test, clichy-prod namespaces. Monitoring and Headlamp are separate cluster tools.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: No alternatives are recorded in a formal ADR. Docker Compose is provided for local Postgres/Redis only, not as a production runtime.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Kubernetes supplies scheduling, service discovery, probes and Deployment rollouts. Operators must manage cluster access, PVCs, secrets, ingress, and node/storage availability. Namespaces isolate names and configuration but do not provide separate cluster failure domains.

docs.title: ADR 0002: PostgreSQL and Prisma
docs.text: Status: Adopted.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The API needs relational persistence for identity, ownership, photo metadata, and processing state.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use PostgreSQL with Prisma schema and committed migrations. Better Auth uses Prisma's PostgreSQL adapter. Each Kubernetes namespace has a CNPG-managed two-instance PostgreSQL cluster; application writes and Prisma migrations use its -rw Service.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: No alternatives are recorded in repository history available here.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Prisma provides typed data access and migration history. Schema migrations must be applied to independent environment databases before rollout and remain backward compatible with old Pods. CNPG replication is configured but not live-verified. Sharding, backups and Test refresh are not implemented; same-node instances do not provide physical host HA.

docs.title: ADR 0003: Redis and BullMQ for photo jobs
docs.text: Status: Adopted for asynchronous photo processing; operational baseline recorded at bce6e50, current live state not checked.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Uploads need image metadata extraction, hashing, and derivative generation without keeping the HTTP request open during all processing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use BullMQ backed by Redis. Server creates queue jobs; worker consumes process-photo; a PostgreSQL outbox stores publication intent and enables retry/recovery.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: No formal comparison is recorded. Synchronous processing was avoided in favor of asynchronous work, based on current architecture.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Retries, backoff, queue identity and recovery behavior are explicit. Redis remains a single instance with AOF/PVC, so it has no configured failover. Shared filesystem access between API and worker is required.

docs.title: ADR 0004: Citus sharding experiment
docs.text: Status: Rejected/abandoned experiment; not current architecture.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Project-provided history says Citus was introduced experimentally to explore PostgreSQL sharding, encountered problems, and was not retained as a validated design.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The current repository uses standard PostgreSQL and does not configure Citus. No operational sharding claims should be made.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Current single PostgreSQL instance is the implemented baseline. A formal comparison or exact experiment commit is not available in the checked-out history reviewed here.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The application has no shard routing or distributed transaction model. Future scaling should start with measured evidence and a documented design. Citus failure root cause and precise experiment outcomes remain unverified.

docs.title: ADR 0005: Traefik as ingress controller
docs.text: Status: Configured by K3s defaults and repository Ingress resources.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Browser traffic needs host/path routing to UI and API, while cluster services remain internal.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use Traefik's traefik IngressClass; base Clichy ingress uses the web entrypoint. K3s installer retains default Traefik installation.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: No controller comparison was found.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: K3s defaults make initial on-premise setup simpler. Hostnames, TLS, DNS and external exposure remain environment-specific; current Clichy Ingress does not configure TLS.

docs.title: ADR 0006: Environment namespaces
docs.text: Status: Adopted in overlays.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Test and Production need distinct settings, credentials and databases; Dev is configured separately.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use namespace-per-environment with independent resources, Secrets, URLs and PostgreSQL databases. CI deploys Test before Production.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Separate clusters are not configured. No formal alternatives record was found.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Namespace separation reduces accidental cross-environment naming/configuration overlap but shares the same cluster/node and does not guarantee resource/failure isolation. Test-to-Production promotion is ordered by workflow dependencies, but explicit application validation/approval depends partly on GitHub Environment settings.

docs.title: ADR 0007: PostgreSQL replication and sharding scope
docs.text: Status: CNPG replication retained in all environments; single-node Citus selected for Test sharding. Multi-node Citus remains deferred.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Assignment asks for replication and sharding. The previous configuration used a single PostgreSQL StatefulSet. The educational prototype remains on one physical K3s node and does not need node-level HA.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use CloudNativePG to manage two PostgreSQL instances per environment with asynchronous physical streaming, separate PVCs, automatic Pod recovery/promotion, and the -rw Service for application connections. Test additionally uses Citus with userId as the distribution key for photo metadata and processing-outbox rows. Dev and Production remain plain CNPG PostgreSQL. Keep replication and sharding as separate concerns. Do not scale database Pods directly.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: A PostgreSQL operator is selected for physical replication. Multi-node Citus was deferred because it introduces worker membership and failure management. A single-node Citus instance in Test provides 32 logical shards and a low-complexity path to validate Citus routing. Synchronous replication is not selected because the prototype does not require zero data loss and asynchronous streaming avoids making writes wait on the standby.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: CNPG remains responsible for the replication exercise. Test Citus has one database Pod and no high availability; the CNPG Test cluster remains deployed separately. The 32 logical shards share one PostgreSQL process and host, so this is not multi-node capacity scaling or failure isolation. The data model uses compound keys containing userId, and outbox jobs carry that key so queries can be routed. Citus and Prisma migrations must stay aligned.

docs.title: ADR 0008: Zero-downtime rollout is not yet verified
docs.text: Status: Open evaluation criterion.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Kubernetes Deployments roll Pods, and deployment scripts wait for rollout completion. Default app replicas are one, and schema changes run before app manifests are updated.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Describe rolling update capability as configured but do not claim zero downtime without an observed test.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Multiple replicas and explicit rollout strategy can improve availability but must account for shared storage and database schema compatibility; no completed demonstration is recorded.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: A controlled deployment test with health checks, concurrent requests, metrics and a migration is needed before claiming the requirement is met.

docs.title: Clichy brand guidelines
docs.text: Clichy is a private home for personal photo collections. The identity should feel calm, personal, carefully organized, and trustworthy; photographs remain the most expressive part of the product.

docs.title: Logo
docs.text:
The symbol combines an open letter C with two offset image frames. The frames suggest a collection without using a literal camera or aperture illustration. Use the full lockup when the wordmark is needed and the symbol for compact places such as the favicon.

Assets live in apps/web/public/brand/:

  • logo-light.svg: charcoal lockup for warm, light surfaces.
  • logo-dark.svg: ivory lockup for dark surfaces.
  • symbol.svg: standalone charcoal symbol.
  • apps/web/public/favicon.svg: standalone symbol for browser and application tabs.
  • apps/web/src/components/brand-logo.tsx: reusable, theme-aware React logo.

Keep the logo at its original proportions, leave clear space around it, and do not recolor, skew, outline, or add effects to the SVG assets. The React logo uses the active theme's foreground and background colors.

docs.title: Color
docs.text:
The palette pairs warm paper and charcoal with a restrained sage accent and a small clay highlight:

Role Light theme Dark theme Use Background Warm ivory Deep warm charcoal Main canvas Foreground Charcoal Soft ivory Text and primary mark Primary Deep sage Light sage Main actions and active navigation Accent Muted clay Soft clay Small highlights, never large surfaces Secondary Pale sage/stone Deep sage/stone Quiet controls and selected surfaces Destructive Accessible red Accessible light red Permanent or destructive actions

Semantic success, warning, border, muted, and focus colors are also defined as CSS variables in packages/ui/src/styles/globals.css. Prefer semantic tokens such as bg-background, text-muted-foreground, and text-destructive over hard-coded colors.

docs.title: Typography
docs.text: Use the existing system sans-serif stack for controls and supporting text, with a restrained serif accent for large collection titles. The UI does not fetch fonts from a third-party host. Keep headings short and legible; use uppercase tracking sparingly for small section labels.

docs.title: Layout and components
docs.text:
• Let the photographs carry color and personality; use quiet surfaces around them.
  • Use consistent, generous spacing, with compact controls near the gallery.
  • Use rounded image corners and soft, rounded controls; avoid nested bordered cards and heavy shadows.
  • Reserve shadows for overlays and transient elevation.
  • Use Lucide icons with consistent stroke weight and pair icons with visible or screen-reader labels.
  • Keep destructive actions explicit and visually distinct.
  • Make focus states visible and preserve comfortable touch targets on mobile.

docs.title: Themes and motion
docs.text: Light and dark modes share the same semantic hierarchy. Use the theme tokens so text, surfaces, borders, and focus rings remain legible in either mode. Avoid theme-specific imagery or color-only status indicators. Honor prefers-reduced-motion; transitions should remain subtle and optional.

docs.title: Local development
docs.text:
Local service orchestration is split: packages/db/docker-compose.yml starts PostgreSQL and Redis; root Turbo scripts run web, server, and worker processes. There is no root Compose file orchestrating all application services.

The expected development sequence is:

pnpm db:start
pnpm db:generate
pnpm db:migrate
pnpm dev

The API listens on port 3000 in apps/server/src/index.ts. The worker exposes health on port 3001. The React Router dev server chooses its local port and reports it at startup. The browser API URL is controlled by VITE_SERVER_URL.

For an isolated service, run pnpm dev:web, pnpm dev:server, or pnpm dev:worker. Keep API and worker pointed at the same PHOTO_STORAGE_PATH; otherwise the worker cannot read originals or the API cannot serve generated derivatives. This local filesystem coordination is also required in Kubernetes.

Use database migration commands for development changes; do not use db:push as a substitute for a committed migration workflow when schema history matters. Use pnpm db:studio to inspect records locally. Local startup has not been executed as part of this documentation pass.

docs.title: 1. Install tools and dependencies
docs.text:
Install Node.js 24, pnpm 12.8.1, Git, and Docker with Compose. Then clone the repository and install dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/valatras/clichy.git
cd clichy
corepack enable
corepack prepare pnpm@12.8.1 --activate
pnpm install

pnpm install triggers Varlock code generation through the root postinstall script. It does not start services.

docs.title: 2. Start local dependencies
docs.text:
pnpm db:start

This invokes the database workspace's docker compose up -d, starting PostgreSQL and Redis with named local volumes. The compose file exposes ports 5432 and 6379 on the host. Its sample PostgreSQL password is for local development only; do not reuse it elsewhere.

Configure local environment files based on the .env.schema files. Use a local PostgreSQL URL targeting database clichy, and set API/worker Redis host to 127.0.0.1. Provide a unique Better Auth secret of at least 32 characters and matching local auth/CORS URLs. Never copy production Secret values.

docs.title: 3. Prepare Prisma and run services
docs.text:
pnpm db:generate
pnpm db:migrate
pnpm dev

db:generate creates the Prisma client. db:migrate runs prisma migrate dev and may prompt to create/apply local migrations. pnpm dev runs package dev tasks through Turbo; use pnpm dev:web, pnpm dev:server, or pnpm dev:worker for an individual service. Confirm Vite's printed URL and that VITE_SERVER_URL points to the API.

docs.title: 4. Useful commands
docs.text:
pnpm check-types
pnpm --filter server test
pnpm --filter worker test
pnpm build
pnpm db:studio
pnpm db:stop
pnpm db:down

These names are defined in root/workspace manifests. db:stop stops containers but preserves volumes; db:down removes Compose containers/network but leaves named volumes unless -v is explicitly passed (which is not part of the script).

For image builds, use the existing Dockerfiles with repository root as build context:

docker build -f infra/docker_clichy_server/Dockerfile -t clichy-server:local .
docker build -f infra/docker_clichy_web/Dockerfile -t clichy-web:local .
docker build -f infra/docker_clichy_worker/Dockerfile -t clichy-worker:local .

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Prisma client missing: run pnpm db:generate after install/schema changes.
  • Connection refused: check docker compose ps in packages/db, then check ports and URLs.
  • Login fails locally: check BETTER_AUTH_URL, CORS_ORIGIN, secret length, and browser API URL alignment.
  • Worker reports no Redis: check Redis host/port/credentials and that worker shares the same queue name as the server.
  • Generated environment types missing: run pnpm env:generate after schema changes.
  • Avoid pnpm db:reset unless you intend to drop and recreate the local database.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
The root package.json pins pnpm@12.8.1; CI uses Node.js 24. The repository uses TypeScript, Turborepo, Varlock, Prisma, and Docker. Local database services are PostgreSQL 18 and Redis 7.4 from packages/db/docker-compose.yml. Docker Compose is needed for those services; Docker/Kubernetes are optional for app-only development.

Versions not pinned in repository metadata (for example, a local kubectl or mkdocs) must be selected by the operator. The K3s bootstrap script is specifically written for Ubuntu Server 24.04 and defaults to K3s v1.37.2+k3s1.

docs.title: Environment files
docs.text:
Schemas are in apps/web/.env.schema, apps/server/.env.schema, apps/worker/.env.schema, and packages/db/.env.schema. Root postinstall runs Varlock code generation. The server/worker require database and Redis connection settings; auth adds BETTER_AUTH_URL, BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, CORS_ORIGIN; web uses VITE_SERVER_URL.

Variable Consumer Meaning/default evidence DATABASE_URL API, worker, Prisma PostgreSQL URL; required by server/worker BETTER_AUTH_SECRET API Required secret, schema min 32 characters BETTER_AUTH_URL API Auth canonical URL CORS_ORIGIN API Allowed browser origin PHOTO_STORAGE_PATH API/worker Defaults in schemas to local data paths; Kubernetes sets /data/photos REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_DB API/worker Defaults in code to 127.0.0.1, 6379, 0 REDIS_PASSWORD, REDIS_TLS API/worker Optional password and TLS toggle PHOTO_QUEUE_NAME API/worker Defaults to photo-processing PHOTO_JOB_ATTEMPTS, PHOTO_JOB_BACKOFF_MS Queue Defaults to 4 and 2000 ms PHOTO_WORKER_CONCURRENCY Worker Default 1; code permits 1 or 2 VITE_SERVER_URL Web build API base URL; currently build workflow supplies localhost URL

Never commit .env files or real secrets. The deploy scripts create Kubernetes Secrets interactively; see namespace setup.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
Path Responsibility apps/web React Router UI apps/server Fastify API, photo storage and processing primitives, metrics, outbox dispatcher apps/worker BullMQ photo processing consumer and health listener packages/auth Better Auth configuration packages/db Prisma schema/client, migrations, local Postgres/Redis Compose packages/jobs Redis connection and BullMQ queue contracts/defaults packages/ui Shared UI components and styles packages/config Shared TypeScript configuration infra/docker_* Service Dockerfiles infra/kubernetes/base Shared Kubernetes resources infra/kubernetes/overlays Dev/Test/Prod Kustomize overlays infra/kubernetes/scripts Cluster, namespace, deployment, migration, monitoring and Headlamp scripts .github/workflows/ci.yml CI, GHCR packaging, Test and Production deploy jobs docs/ MkDocs source plus existing design/operations documentation

The root is a pnpm workspace coordinated by Turborepo. Package scripts are authoritative for runnable commands; consult package.json files before using a command not listed here.

docs.title: Testing and build checks
docs.text:
The repository uses Node's built-in test runner through tsx. Server tests cover storage, metrics, image processing, photo queries/routes, and outbox dispatch. Worker tests cover job processing behavior.

pnpm check-types
pnpm --filter server test
pnpm --filter worker test
pnpm build

CI uses the same commands after pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, with Node 24. Type checking receives a placeholder DATABASE_URL and web server URL; tests/build may depend on package environment configuration. The workflow does not run a dedicated lint task despite a root Turbo lint task definition.

For focused debugging, execute a package test file, for example pnpm --filter server exec tsx --test src/image-processing.test.ts. The server and worker test suites and type checks are run as part of the local validation for changes to the asynchronous photo pipeline.

docs.title: CI/CD pipeline
docs.text:
The single workflow is .github/workflows/ci.yml, triggered by pushes and pull requests to master.

flowchart TD
  Push[Push or PR to master] --> CI[Install frozen deps; typecheck; server tests; worker tests; build]
  CI -->|success| Images[Build server/web/worker images]
  Images -->|push to master| GHCR[Publish sha-<commit> tags]
  Images -->|PR| BuildOnly[Build only, no publish]
  GHCR --> Test[Self-hosted runner: verify SHA + single valtask node]
  Test --> TestMigrate[Prisma migrate deploy to Test]
  TestMigrate --> TestApply[Apply Test manifests and await rollouts]
  TestApply --> ProdDispatch{Manual workflow dispatch with deploy_prod=true?}
  ProdDispatch -->|yes| ProdGate[GitHub production Environment]
  ProdGate --> ProdMigrate[Prisma migrate deploy to Production]
  ProdMigrate --> ProdApply[Apply Production manifests and await rollouts]

docs.title: Sequence and gates
docs.text:
1. CI uses GitHub-hosted Ubuntu, pnpm action, Node 24 and frozen lockfile. It runs pnpm check-types, server tests, worker tests, and pnpm build.
  2. Packaging builds three Docker images from root context and service Dockerfiles. Only push-to-master logs into GHCR and pushes tags ghcr.io/valatras/clichy-{server,web,worker}:sha-${GITHUB_SHA}. Pull requests build without publishing.
  3. Test deploy runs on a self-hosted Linux runner. It requires checked-out SHA to equal workflow SHA and exactly one cluster node named valtask. It applies monitoring manifests, runs deploy.sh test sha-..., and reports resources even on failure.
  4. Pushes deploy Test only. Production requires manually dispatching the workflow on master with deploy_prod=true; that run rebuilds, redeploys Test, then uses GitHub Environment production and the same exact-SHA checks before deploying prod.
  5. deploy.sh invokes migration first. If migration fails, application manifests are not applied. On success it renders the overlay with the SHA, applies it, then waits up to five minutes for server, web, and worker rollouts.

GitHub Environment review/approval is not configured in the YAML; it may be configured in repository settings. Production's manual dispatch gate prevents a Test push from automatically changing Prod. There is no separate Test smoke-test step or automatic rollback job. A failing rollout stops the job, but rollback is an operator action. No zero-downtime demonstration is included.

docs.title: Migration workflow detail
docs.text: deploy.sh waits for the environment CNPG Cluster. For Test, it also applies and waits for the standalone Citus Deployment. migrate.sh verifies a clean checked-out source, verifies node valtask, reads the environment Secret's DATABASE_URL without printing it, port-forwards the environment's database Service to an ephemeral loopback port, performs a PostgreSQL protocol SELECT 1, then invokes prisma migrate deploy (or prisma migrate status). Test migrations additionally register the photo and outbox tables as Citus-distributed; Dev and Production use CNPG. For the loopback-only port-forward it sets sslmode=disable so Prisma and the node-postgres probe use the same protocol. It unsets credentials and cleans up the port-forward. Migrations run before new app manifests, so they must remain compatible with currently running code during that interval.

docs.title: Cloud migration plan (not yet tested)
docs.text: There is no cloud-specific overlay or validated provider deployment in the repository. This page is a planning checklist, not an executable runbook.

docs.title: Portable parts
docs.text: Container images and tags, application Deployments, Services, Prisma migration model, queue contract, health endpoints, and most Kustomize structure are portable. The CI workflow can publish images to GHCR independent of runtime provider, but its self-hosted runner and kubeconfig currently target a host named valtask and enforce a single node.

docs.title: Provider-dependent work
docs.text: Area Current assumption Migration decision/work Storage Local PVs/node paths in Prod; local-path in other cluster Choose CSI block/file storage, access modes, snapshots, encryption, reclaim behavior; migrate data and validate API/worker shared photo access. PostgreSQL CNPG two-instance physical streaming cluster with two node-local PVCs per environment Decide managed database vs CNPG on cloud; select CSI-backed storage, topology/anti-affinity, backups, secrets, networking and supported Kubernetes/PostgreSQL versions; migrate/restore data and validate Prisma connectivity. Redis Single in-cluster Redis with PVC/AOF Decide managed Redis or replicated service; update TLS/auth and availability behavior. Ingress/load balancer K3s Traefik, host-based rules Choose managed LB/controller, configure health checks, public/private access, TLS and forwarding headers. DNS Local/LAN and existing hostname config Set authoritative records and certificate issuance; validate auth callback/CORS origin. Secrets Kubernetes Secrets made by scripts Move to cloud secret manager or sealed/external secret controller; rotate secrets and limit access. Registry GHCR Configure cloud cluster pull access and image policy; keep immutable SHA references. Monitoring kube-prometheus-stack with PVCs Size persistent metrics, retention, alert routing, egress and external monitoring needs. Network single-node K3s and ClusterIP services Design subnets, firewall rules, egress, private DB access, and pod/service CIDRs. Cost/sizing small fixed resource requests/limits Load test image processing and storage; size CPU, memory, IOPS, snapshots, egress and HA by measured demand.

docs.title: Safe migration sequence to design
docs.text:
1. Select provider and decide managed vs in-cluster PostgreSQL/Redis.
  2. Provision cluster, CSI storage, secrets integration, ingress, DNS and monitoring in a separate environment.
  3. Build and push a pinned SHA image; apply schema migrations using a reviewed compatible migration.
  4. Restore a sanitized Test dataset and verify auth, uploads, derivatives, queue recovery, metrics, and rollback procedure.
  5. Plan photo file migration and database consistency checks; preserve originals and verify hashes.
  6. Exercise failover, backup restore, rolling update and zero-downtime criteria before any production cutover.

These steps require environment-specific manifests and operational validation before becoming a production procedure.

docs.title: Scope and prerequisites
docs.text:
infra/kubernetes/scripts/install-k3s.sh targets Ubuntu Server 24.04, installs the K3s version declared by K3S_VERSION (default v1.37.2+k3s1), and retains K3s defaults including Traefik and local-path storage. It creates a user-owned kubeconfig (default ~/.kube/config-k3s) with mode 0600. It does not configure firewall rules, SSH, a multi-node cluster, or cloud resources.

Other scripts install Helm, prepare namespaces/secrets, install monitoring, configure LAN access, and install Headlamp. Read each script and confirm the selected kube context before running it: several scripts prompt before mutation, and namespace preparation for Production requires a mounted /srv/clichy filesystem.

docs.title: On-premise flow
docs.text:
1. Prepare an Ubuntu 24.04 host and verify storage/network prerequisites.
  2. Run infra/kubernetes/scripts/install-k3s.sh as the non-root operator account.
  3. Set KUBECONFIG to the generated kubeconfig and confirm kubectl get nodes.
  4. Install Helm with infra/kubernetes/scripts/install-helm.sh if needed.
  5. Prepare each namespace with infra/kubernetes/scripts/prepare-namespace.sh dev|test|prod; this creates local secret files and Kubernetes Secrets.
  6. Install monitoring with infra/kubernetes/scripts/install-monitoring.sh.
  7. Deploy application through CI or the exact SHA deploy script; details are in deployment.

The scripts are operational instructions, not proof that a clean host bootstrap was recently exercised. Production local PV manifests require node valtask and paths under /srv/clichy/k3s-storage/prod; generic cloud/local clusters do not satisfy these assumptions.

docs.title: Local development cluster
docs.text: The Dev overlay targets clichy.localhost, local/dev image tags, and one replica each. The repository does not provide a dedicated local cluster creation tool beyond K3s installer and the Dev Kustomize overlay. Build and load images into a chosen cluster yourself; this exact workflow is not automated in repository scripts.

docs.title: Kubernetes implementation
docs.text: Kustomize base resources are under infra/kubernetes/base; environment overlays are under infra/kubernetes/overlays/{dev,test,prod}. Common resources include web/API/worker Deployments, Services, Redis Deployment/Service/PVC, photo PVC, Ingress, and an environment-specific CNPG Cluster. Install the pinned CNPG operator once in cnpg-system before preparing any application namespace.

docs.title: Workload behavior
docs.text:
• API and web use readiness/liveness HTTP checks on /; worker has /ready and /live probes on port 3001.
  • CNPG runs two PostgreSQL 18.6 instances per namespace and provisions a separate 2 GiB PVC per instance. Dev and Production applications use clichy-postgres-rw. Test also runs a single-node Citus database with its own PVC; the Test application uses clichy-citus-rw for user-sharded photo tables while CNPG remains available for replication exercises.
  • Redis uses a one-replica Deployment, AOF, noeviction, 256 MiB maxmemory, probes, and a PVC.
  • API, worker, web and database have CPU/memory requests and limits in base manifests.
  • Test adds CPU HPA for API and web (1–4 replicas, 70% utilization target). Dev and Production specify one replica for web/server/worker. Production does not include this HPA.
  • The namespace preparation script applies each CNPG Cluster and waits for its Ready condition. The deploy script waits for the database Cluster to be Ready before migrations, then applies app manifests and waits for each app Deployment rollout.

Kubernetes Deployment rollout is not itself proof of zero downtime. One-replica app workloads, storage attachment, readiness behavior, schema compatibility, and live traffic need a measured rollout test. CNPG's two replicas share the one valtask node and do not provide host-level HA.

docs.title: Environment differences
docs.text:
Dev uses clichy.localhost, development NODE_ENV, and local image names. Test uses clichy-test.home.arpa, GHCR images, hardened app security context, image pull secret, and HPA. Production uses valtask.xyz, exact SHA image tags, hardened contexts, production secrets, local PVs and one replica. All share the base architecture while namespaces and Secrets isolate resources.

Render without applying to inspect an overlay:

kubectl kustomize infra/kubernetes/overlays/test

This requires kubectl with Kustomize support. Do not apply a rendered overlay until its namespace, secrets, image references, storage, and target cluster are reviewed.

docs.title: Prometheus, Grafana, and alerts
docs.text:
infra/kubernetes/scripts/install-monitoring.sh installs the pinned kube-prometheus-stack chart in namespace monitoring. It provides Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, kube-state-metrics, node-exporter and the Kubernetes resource metrics API through Metrics Server. Prometheus retains seven days of metrics. Grafana's sidecar imports the versioned Clichy Photo Service dashboard from the labelled ConfigMap.

Prometheus discovers three application metric sources:

  • ServiceMonitor/clichy-server scrapes the API /metrics endpoint every 30 seconds in Dev, Test and Prod. It includes HTTP request rate, status, duration and active-request metrics, plus the number of unpublished PostgreSQL outbox events.
  • PodMonitor/clichy-worker scrapes worker /metrics every 15 seconds in all three namespaces. It exports BullMQ counts by state, completed-job and failed-attempt rates, job duration, and whether the queue metrics query is succeeding.
  • PodMonitor/clichy-postgres scrapes CNPG's PostgreSQL metrics port in all three namespaces.

The PrometheusRules alert on replica WAL/lag issues, worker/outbox backlogs, missing worker metric scrapes, restarts, unavailable deployments, image/crash backoff, sustained CPU/memory use, low PVC space and Test HPAs that remain at their replica ceiling. Alert rules and dashboard queries consume collected metrics; they do not make a missing scrape work. Verify actual targets and series after each monitoring or worker change.

From valtask, inspect configuration and target resources:

kubectl get pods,services -n monitoring -o wide
kubectl get servicemonitors,podmonitors,prometheusrules -n monitoring
kubectl get servicemonitor clichy-server -n monitoring -o yaml
kubectl get podmonitor clichy-worker -n monitoring -o yaml
kubectl get podmonitor clichy-postgres -n monitoring -o yaml
kubectl get prometheusrule clichy-alerts -n monitoring -o yaml

In Grafana at http://valtask:3000, open Clichy Photo Service, choose clichy-test, and check HTTP rate/p95, worker queue state, outbox backlog, HPA desired/current replicas, CPU and memory, PVC capacity and PostgreSQL replication panels. In Prometheus, check Status → Targets for the API, worker and both CNPG Pods. A missing target or empty panel is not evidence that the workload is idle until scrape health is confirmed.

The API and worker image changes must first be deployed to Test so the new /metrics series exist. The ordinary Test workflow applies infra/kubernetes/monitoring; it does not reinstall or upgrade the Helm release. Do not run install-monitoring.sh as a routine apply: if the Helm release already exists, the installer requires an explicit reviewed upgrade.

docs.title: HPA behavior
docs.text:
Test has CPU HPAs for clichy-server and clichy-web, target 70% of the requested CPU, minimum one and maximum four replicas. The request is 100m CPU for each container, so a 70% target corresponds to 70m average usage per Pod. The HPA requires working Metrics Server data and CPU requests. Prometheus metrics alone do not supply the metrics.k8s.io API used by HPA.

The worker has no HPA. Redis and CNPG are also not HPA-scaled. Do not manually scale a Deployment that has an HPA attached; the controller will reconcile its replica count. A worker is suitable for the manual scaling demonstration because it has no HPA:

NS=clichy-test
kubectl scale deployment/clichy-worker -n "$NS" --replicas=2
kubectl rollout status deployment/clichy-worker -n "$NS" --timeout=180s
kubectl get deployment clichy-worker -n "$NS" -o wide
kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -l app=clichy-worker -o wide

# Restore the configured Test count after recording the demonstration.
kubectl scale deployment/clichy-worker -n "$NS" --replicas=1
kubectl rollout status deployment/clichy-worker -n "$NS" --timeout=180s

This temporarily increases CPU/memory use and consumers of the shared photos PVC. Check kubectl top nodes first and restore one replica after recording the result.

docs.title: Reproducible Test load
docs.text:
First confirm that Metrics Server works and both HPAs have valid metrics:

kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -n clichy-test
kubectl get hpa -n clichy-test -o wide
kubectl describe hpa clichy-server -n clichy-test
kubectl describe hpa clichy-web -n clichy-test

If HPA metrics show <unknown>, fix Metrics Server or the Pod CPU request before generating load. Then run the repository script from valtask in an interactive terminal:

./infra/kubernetes/scripts/load-test-test.sh server 300 32

The script verifies the current context is the single-node valtask, displays current resource use, asks before starting, and port-forwards to the Test API. It sends read-only unauthenticated GET /photos requests (expected response: 401), so it does not upload photos or create records. The request driver runs on valtask, outside the application Pod cgroups. To drive the web HPA instead, use:

./infra/kubernetes/scripts/load-test-test.sh web 300 32

Use a second terminal while the load runs:

kubectl get hpa -n clichy-test -w
kubectl get deployments,pods -n clichy-test -o wide
kubectl top pods -n clichy-test

Capture HPA current/desired replicas, CPU utilization, Pod readiness and Grafana HTTP rate/CPU panels. The HPA and Metrics Server sampling delays mean scaling may take a minute or more. If the selected HPA remains at one replica and CPU stays below target, stop the run and increase concurrency or duration within the script limits; never run this generator against Prod. After the load ends, keep watching until HPA returns to one replica.

If metrics are unavailable, inspect HPA events and requests:

kubectl describe hpa clichy-server -n clichy-test
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -o wide
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -n clichy-test
kubectl get deployment clichy-server -n clichy-test \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.template.spec.containers[*]}{.name}{" cpu-request="}{.resources.requests.cpu}{"\n"}{end}'

One-node scaling demonstrates Kubernetes replica behavior; it does not add host-level availability or capacity beyond the resources of valtask.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  Public[Browser: valtask.xyz / www.valtask.xyz] --> CF[Cloudflare reverse proxy]
  CF --> Tunnel[cloudflared Tunnel]
  subgraph Cluster[K3s cluster]
    subgraph Dev[clichy-dev]
      D[web + server + worker + CNPG primary + standby + Redis]
    end
    subgraph Test[clichy-test]
      T[web + server + worker + CNPG primary + standby + Redis + HPA]
    end
    subgraph Prod[clichy-prod]
      P[web + server + worker + CNPG primary + standby + Redis]
    end
    subgraph Monitoring[monitoring]
      M[Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager]
    end
    subgraph Headlamp[headlamp]
      H[Headlamp UI]
    end
    Traefik[Cluster Traefik]
  end
  Tunnel -->|HTTP to Traefik web :80; www canonicalized by Cloudflare| Traefik
  Traefik -->|host rules| Dev
  Traefik -->|host rules| Test
  Traefik -->|valtask.xyz| Prod
  M -. scrapes app and database metrics .-> Dev
  M -. scrapes app and database metrics .-> Test
  M -. scrapes app and database metrics .-> Prod

Each clichy-* namespace contains independent workload Services, database, Redis, generated ConfigMaps, and environment Secrets. There is no data replication between namespaces. Monitoring ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor resources select all three environments; actual production metric visibility still depends on successful installation and scrape health.

Production's public route is proxied by Cloudflare for valtask.xyz and www.valtask.xyz, then enters through the Cloudflare Tunnel to Traefik; www.valtask.xyz redirects at Cloudflare to canonical valtask.xyz. The tunnel and redirect are external configuration and are not represented as Kubernetes resources in this repository.

headlamp has separate RBAC and Ingress manifests. The Monitoring/Headlamp manifests and scripts configure cluster tools; inspect their LAN hostnames and access policy before exposing them.

docs.title: Setup and inspection
docs.text:
infra/kubernetes/scripts/prepare-namespace.sh test
kubectl get all,pvc,ingress -n clichy-test
kubectl get secret -n clichy-test

Secret listing shows names only. Do not print Secret data into logs or paste it into documentation. The setup script asks for database and GHCR credentials and stores a local protected env file under $HOME/.config/clichy.

docs.title: Claims and paths
docs.text:
CNPG creates two independent 2 GiB PostgreSQL PVCs per environment, one per instance. Dev/Test use the cluster's local-path class. Production declares two pre-bound 2 GiB PVs under /srv/clichy/k3s-storage/prod/postgres-cnpg-{1,2}, using clichy-prod-local, Retain and node affinity to valtask. The legacy 10 GiB PostgreSQL PV and directory remain reserved for the old StatefulSet until manual cutover validation; they are not used by CNPG. The photos PVC remains 10 GiB and Redis 1 GiB.

The namespace preparation script checks /srv/clichy is mounted and creates the two new CNPG paths only when empty, owned by UID/GID 26. It does not alter the legacy database path. The supplied valtask report shows 28 GiB available on this 30 GiB filesystem; two logical 2 GiB PVC capacities do not reserve filesystem blocks, so monitor actual host and PVC usage as data grows. A full filesystem can stop both instances at once.

The server and worker mount the photos claim at /data/photos. They must see the same files. Access mode is ReadWriteOnce; this is often node-scoped rather than multi-node shared storage, and does not establish safe cross-node scheduling. Production is explicitly tied to one node.

docs.title: Operational checks
docs.text:
kubectl get pvc,pv -n clichy-prod -o wide
kubectl describe pvc clichy-server-photos -n clichy-prod
kubectl get cluster,pods,pvc -n clichy-prod -o wide
